name: NVSwitch 3 (Hopper, H100/H200 - contested generation number)
version: NVSwitch 3 / 'NVLink 4 Switch' - NVIDIA publishes two different generation numbers for the same silicon
bandwidth_basis: PER GPU, PER DIRECTION, CONTESTED GENERATION NUMBER. BANDWIDTH IS NOT IN DISPUTE: 450 GB/s per direction is forced by the same 900 GB/s bidirectional per-GPU figure that nvswitch-4 carries, and NVIDIA's own Hopper developer blog states 'a system with eight NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPUs features 3.6 TB/s of bisection bandwidth and 450 GB/s of bandwidth for reduction operations' (net2-nvidia-nvswitch3-blog). 3.6 TB/s of bisection across 8 GPUs is 450 GB/s per GPU, and the blog's separate '450 GB/s of bandwidth for reduction operations' is the SHARP in-network-reduction rate - so 450 is both the per-GPU fabric rate and the reduction rate. WHAT IS CONTESTED IS THE NAME: NVIDIA's technical blog calls the Hopper switch 'third-generation NVIDIA NVSwitch', while the NVLink/NVLink Switch specification table labels the same part 'NVLink 4 Switch' paired with 'Fourth Generation' NVLink (link-nvlink-switch-spec). Both are first-party and both are in current NVIDIA materials. This is a pure vendor-naming disagreement with no numerical consequence, so per this repo's rules both labels are retained rather than one being chosen. Practical reading: NVIDIA numbered the switch generation separately from the link generation (Volta=1, Ampere=2, Hopper=3), while the spec table aligns switch generation with link generation (Hopper link 4 => '4 Switch'). See nvswitch-1 and nvswitch-2 for the same trap on other generations - on A100 the link is NVLink 3 but the switch is NVSwitch 2.
topology: Switched, non-blocking all-to-all across the 8-GPU domain inside one server, as at NVSwitch 2 and 4. The Hopper generation's real additions are in-network compute and management rather than topology: SHARP in-network reduction and multicast, control-plane resilience, and the ability to run a partially populated rack.
switching: Third-generation NVSwitch is where SHARP ARRIVES ON THE NVIDIA SCALE-UP SIDE. NVIDIA's Hopper architecture page states 'Third-Generation NVIDIA NVSwitch supports Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol (SHARP) in-network computing, previously only available on InfiniBand, and provides a 2X increase in all-reduce throughput within eight H200 or H100 GPU servers compared to the previous-generation A100 Tensor Core GPU systems'. The 2x all-reduce claim is the directly relevant number for TP: SHARP moves the reduction into the switch, which attacks exactly the cost that docs/11-interconnect-decision.md measures.
notes: The Hopper-generation switch, added 2026-10-03 to complete the 1/2/3/4/5 ladder. It was genuinely missing, and its absence was actively misleading: the repo had nvswitch-2 (A100) and nvswitch-4 (H100) with no Hopper record, which invites a reader to conclude the switch was skipped between Ampere and Hopper. It was not. UNRESOLVED VENDOR NAMING, both first-party and both retained: NVIDIA's developer blog titles its Hopper switch discussion 'Upgrading Multi-GPU Interconnectivity with the Third-Generation NVIDIA NVSwitch', while NVIDIA's NVLink/NVLink Switch specification table labels the same Hopper switch 'NVLink 4 Switch' with the bandwidth row 'NVLink Switch GPU-to-GPU Bandwidth 900 GB/s' and 'Total Aggregate Bandwidth 7.2 TB/s' - identical to the NVSwitch 4 row. Two current first-party NVIDIA documents therefore disagree on whether this part is the 3rd or the 4th generation. No bandwidth impact: both give 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, and this record stores the halved 450 per direction. THE DECISION-RELEVANT FACT IS SHARP, not the name: NVIDIA's Hopper architecture page credits third-generation NVSwitch with 'a 2X increase in all-reduce throughput within eight H200 or H100 GPU servers compared to the previous-generation A100 systems' - the first NVIDIA scale-up part to do in-network reduction, previously an InfiniBand-only feature. That 2x is the same axis as the B* crossover in docs/11-interconnect-decision.md, and the two compose: H100's raw 450 GB/s per direction already puts the TP all-reduce crossover at B* ~3,318 on 7B geometry, so SHARP reduces a cost that is already negligible at typical serving batch, and its value shows up instead at high batch or high TP degree where B* is being approached. NVIDIA's separate inference blog (link-nvlink-nvswitch-inference-blog) reports up to 1.5x higher throughput for Llama 3.1 70B on H200 with NVSwitch versus point-to-point - the topology effect, which is separate from and smaller than the SHARP effect.
